reviews.body: A bunch of comments here. At a high level, I'm not sure the union is the right approach. I'd like to see an estimate of the actual size of an ESNIKeys record for a typical CDN.

comments.body: What's failure fallback?

This doesn't seem like quite the right requirement. I think I would try to set the problem up first.

"There are deployment environments in which a domain is served by multiple server operators who do not sure the ESNI Keys. Because ESNIKeys and A/AAAA lookup are independent, it is therefore possible to obtain an ESNIKeys record which does not match the A/AAAA records. Naively using this record would result in handshake failure. The design of the system must therefore allow clients to detect and recover from this situation."
This seems like good advice, but why is it just for split mode? And why does it belong here?
I think I actually covered this above.
These masks should be a length.
Cool people have a length field here so you can skip unknown types.
This seems like it needs to be unpacked. Like, why is this OK.
ITYM CIDR.

Oh, this is an interesting catch. Say that I go to ```www.example.com``` and I get ```alt.example.com```. You're saying that I lookup:

```
alt.example.com? A/AAAA
www.example.com? ESNIKeys
```

So, I'm actually not sure that this is the right answer, as it depends on how alt-svc is being used. Consider the case where the origin is pointing to a CDN. Don't we want the CDN's ESNIKeys to control?

In either case, you should use "origin" and "alternative"
these queries -> ESNI queries.
Let's not get into an IPv6/IPv4 debate here.
I think you need a more concrete algorithm here, and to be clearer about what you want.

I'm not sure that this algorithm is quite what we want. 

Stepping back, I think you want something like this:

1. If you get ESNIKeys and it's got a full address, use the address.
2. If you get A or AAAA, wait up to X seconds for ESNIKeys and then if you don't get it, proceed without. If you do get it, and it's got a full address, use that, as in (2).
3. If you have ESNIKeys and either A or AAAA and the address mask matches, then use that address and ESNIKeys, possibly waiting for up to Y seconds if you have only A or AAAA and prefer the other type of address.
4. If you have ESNIKeys and either A or AAAA and the address mask doesn't match then issue a query for the Hostname and that type of address.
5. If you do all the queries mentioned above and you still don't have an address match, then error.

I don't think you need the CNAME comparisons. How do they help?
Fallback to plaintext SNI.

What value would the netmask serve? If A/AAAA and ESNI mismatch occurs frequently, then a mask is insufficient. If it doesn't occur frequently, then including anything but a full address seems less optimal. I would prefer to keep this simple here.
This is one way in which folks can write an extension draft specifying the netmask. I do not think that should be done here.

Two values:
* Using netmask is a space efficient way of representing multiple addresses. Organizations running servers at mass-scale often setup multiple servers (serving same set of origins) within a single network address. I think it's important to keep the size of the structure (and hence the DNS record) small.
* Organizations often install new servers within a pre-allocated network address. Having netmask in the ESNI record removes the necessity to update the ESNI record every time a new server is being installed.

pulls.title: Initial PSK binding proposal.
pulls.author: dvorak42
pulls.body:
This adds the PSK binding via a custom PSK identity associated with extensions. Maybe a more general version would be useful to stick somewhere so that any extension which wants to do a binding doesn't need to hack it in?

Additional changes:
- Remove label swapping, since the PSK ClientHello binding should be sufficient to prevent reuse.
- Remove the AAD of KeyShareClientHello since the PSK ClientHello binding should be sufficient.
- Since now the encrypted_sni extension doesn't change at all as a result of HRR, simplify the wording to make sure the whole extension doesn't change. (server might not actually need to check if doesn't change, it just needs to be consistent in the processing of the extension, ignoring CH1 entirely, but saying it checks it doesn't change seems simplest.)

The naming/formatting of the Client Hello Binding section probably could use some work, not sure how to indicate that this is a hack onto an existing extension. (There was a nicer structure where there was a single PSK identity for extensions, and then we had a struct embedded in the PskBinderEntry, but it looks like the max PskBinderEntry size is 255 bytes, which is kind of limiting, though maybe doable if we think no more than 7 extensions will play these binding games.)

comments.body: nit: We probably need to wrap this in "~~~"
I wonder if folks will complain about possible identity collisions. The binders won't be the same since we use `encrypted_sni_binder_key` below, so perhaps it's not an issue?

I'm hoping that we don't have accidental identity collisions (a real PSK with an identity of CHExtff07. An attacker could swap in their own PSK binder, but without knowing the encrypted_sni_binder_key, they shouldn't be able to generate a passing binder.

To have it written down somewhere, an alternative construction is having a single identity for all extensions, and then making the binder be a sequence of extension_type, binder pairs, but since the binders are limited to 255 bytes, that doesn't really extend very far. (Though I guess we could just stuff multiple extensions CHExtensionBinder1, CHExtensionBinder2, ..., but that seems hacky for a savings of a few bytes).

Nit: markdown anchor name

I think this paragraph needs help.  With HTTPSSVC, an ESNIConfig is never used with the "independent" A/AAA lookups.  Rather, the ESNIConfig is only used in conjunction with IP addresses that were identified (directly or indirectly) by the HTTPSSVC record.

In HTTPSSVC terminology, I think the requirement you're getting at is: When publishing an HTTPSSVC record containing an ESNI public key, the publisher MUST ensure that all IP addresses of SvcDomainName correspond to servers that have access to the corresponding private key or are authoritative for the fallback domain.  (This requirement seems pretty obvious to me, but there might be an argument for stating it more explicitly in the SVCB draft.)

As the name suggests, HTTPSSVC is HTTPS-specific, whereas ESNI is presumably applicable to TLS generally.  As such, it seems a little odd to see it covered in detail here.  At a minimum, a sentence clarifying that this section is specific to HTTPS would seem appropriate.  Alternatively, this could be rephrased in terms of SVCB.
